newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus sees lower 1996 growth, rebound in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus sees lower 1996 growth, rebound in 1997.

text.p: A decline in tourism arrivals in Cyprus and increased tension on the divided island will cut growth in gross domestic product to 2.5 percent in 1996 from five percent in 1995, but growth is expected to rebound to about 3.5 percent in 1997, Finance Minister Christodoulos Christodoulou said on Friday.
"Cyprus's economy faced difficulties and unpredictable problems which affected its performance," he told members of a parliamentary committee charged with making recomendations for the 1997 budget.
It is the second consecutive year that the eastern Mediterranean island's economy showed a slower growth rate. The rate fell to five percent in 1995 from six percent in 1994.
Just four months ago the finance ministry had predicted the growth rate this year would be 3.8 percent.
Christodoulou said the rate was still higher than other European countries, adding that prospects for 1997 are encouraging. Growth is expected to be about 3.5 percent in 1997, he said.

Unemployment is reflecting the slowdown, with the rated expected to edge upwards to three percent in 1997 compared to 2.6 percent in 1996. Inflation is expected to exactly match unemployment, at 3.0 percent in 1997 compared with 2.6 percent in 1996.
Tourism arrivals, on which the island heavily depends, were down by four percent until mid-August compared with the same period last year.

"The relative slowdown is due mainly to a decline in the rate of growth internally and to a reduction in tourism demand.... The development of the economy was also negatively affected by external factors, like the slowdown of economic development in the European Union and internationally," he said.
Christodoulou said tension which increased on the island after the killings of two Greek Cypriots in August by people from the Turkish held areas of the island also took its toll.
Turkey has occupied the northern parts of the island since it invaded in 1974 in the wake of a short-lived coup engineered by the then military government in Greece.
In 1997 the fiscal deficit is expected to reach 176.2 million pounds ($377.06 million) or four percent of GDP compared to 119 million, or 2.9 percent of GDP, forecast for 1996.
Public debt is expected to reach 2.36 billion or 54.2 percent of GDP in 1997 compared with the forecast for 1996 of 2.04 billion, or 55.2 percent of GDP. ($=0.467 pounds)
